1. Core Clinical Tension: The core clinical tension centers on a 26-year-old previously healthy, immunocompetent male presenting with a 12-day subacute febrile prodrome, persistent headache, photosensitivity, diplopia, and progressive encephalopathy (GCS 13) complicated by refractory hyponatremia and secondary acute collapse with seizures, cranial nerve palsy, and obstructive hydrocephalus. The central diagnostic dilemma is distinguishing tuberculous meningitis (TBM)—which typically produces thick gelatinous basal leptomeningeal exudates entrapping cranial nerves and obstructing CSF outflow—from acute or partially treated pyogenic bacterial meningitis, fungal meningitis (specifically Cryptococcus neoformans in immunocompetent hosts), viral meningoencephalitis, and non-infectious inflammatory disorders such as neurosarcoidosis.

2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is established at the emergence of obstructive hydrocephalus and basilar enhancement on contrast-enhanced neuroimaging alongside the baseline clinical and CSF profile, strictly before revealing the definitive diagnostic score/label (probable tuberculous meningitis), antitubercular pharmacotherapy (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol), or procedural mortality. The case prompt presents the complete admission narrative: 12-day prodrome of fever, headache, nausea, diplopia, drowsy mental state (GCS 13), mild neck stiffness, oculomotor deficit, baseline triage labs, normal chest radiograph, CSF findings (clear, lymphocytic pleocytosis, protein >2 g/L, glucose <50% serum ratio), and repeat contrast CT revealing ventriculomegaly with basal meningeal enhancement.

3. Differential Distinctions: Distinctive clinical pivots include the subacute 12-day indolent tempo, moderate CSF pleocytosis (40 cells/µL) with clear fluid and lymphocytic predominance, marked CSF protein elevation (2.09 g/L) coupled with severe hypoglycorrhachia (40 mg/dL, <50% serum ratio), progressive hyponatremia (126 to 124 mmol/L from SIADH/cerebral salt wasting), cranial nerve III involvement, and hallmark basilar meningeal enhancement with tri-ventricular dilation. Pyogenic bacterial meningitis is ruled out by the subacute timeline, normal blood WBC, lack of cloudy/purulent fluid or neutrophilic pleocytosis, and lack of response to ceftriaxone. Cryptococcal meningitis is unlikely given non-reactive HIV serology, immunocompetent status, and classic basal predilection. Viral meningoencephalitis is ruled out by profound hypoglycorrhachia and basilar exudative hydrocephalus. Neurosarcoidosis is excluded by sustained high fevers, severe CSF hypoglycorrhachia, and an absence of pulmonary/mediastinal pathology on chest radiography.
case_prompt:
A 26-year-old male is admitted to the hospital with persistent fever and altered mental status. He reports a 12-day history of high fevers (38–39 °C), progressively worsening headaches, nausea and vomiting, photosensitivity, diplopia, and severe fatigue. Relatives confirm he is self-employed, a mild cigarette smoker, does not drink alcohol, and denies any history of illicit drug use.

In the emergency department, the patient is drowsy and febrile with a body temperature of 38.0 °C and a heart rate of 110 beats per minute. He denies chest discomfort or palpitations. His admission Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score is 13. There is no cutaneous rash, petechiae, or ecchymosis. Cardiovascular, pulmonary, and abdominal examinations are entirely unremarkable. Neurological examination reveals drowsiness, mild neck stiffness on forward flexion without overt Kernig or Brudzinski signs, and focal cranial nerve signs manifesting as diplopia and an oculomotor (third nerve) palsy.

Triage laboratory evaluation reveals: white blood cell count 5.8 × 10^9/L (with 89.5% neutrophils and 3.1% lymphocytes), hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, platelet count 243 × 10^9/L, serum sodium 126 mmol/L, serum potassium 4.0 mmol/L, and random blood glucose 134 mg/dL. Blood cultures show no bacterial growth. Diagnostic serologies for human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), cytomegalovirus (CMV), and Toxoplasma gondii IgM are all negative. Initial chest radiography indicates no parenchymal pathology or localized consolidation, and an initial non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain is unremarkable.

Lumbar puncture yields grossly clear cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Analysis of the CSF reveals a white blood cell count of 40 cells/µL with lymphocytic predominance, red blood cells of 16 cells/µL, markedly elevated protein concentration of 2.09 g/L, and a depressed glucose concentration of 40 mg/dL (cerebrospinal fluid-to-serum glucose ratio less than 50%).

The patient is admitted to the inpatient ward and started on supportive care, intravenous broad-spectrum cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g/day), intravenous dexamethasone, hypertonic saline for hyponatremia, and antipyretics. Over the following days, despite therapy, his severe headache and third nerve palsy persist, and his serum sodium drops further to 124 mmol/L. One week into hospitalization, the patient suffers an acute neurological decompensation characterized by sudden loss of consciousness and seizures. A repeat contrast-enhanced CT scan of the brain demonstrates prominent basilar meningeal enhancement along with marked ventriculomegaly involving the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles, consistent with obstructive hydrocephalus.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis) typically follows an abrupt, hyperacute course (<24–48 hours) marked by high peripheral leukocytosis, cloudy or purulent CSF with marked polymorphonuclear (neutrophilic) pleocytosis (usually >1,000 cells/µL), and profound hypoglycorrhachia. In this patient, the subacute 12-day prodrome, normal peripheral white blood cell count (5.8 × 10^9/L), clear CSF with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (40 cells/µL), sterile blood cultures, failure to improve on intravenous ceftriaxone, and late development of basal enhancement with hydrocephalus rule out typical pyogenic bacterial meningitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: clear appearance, increased white cell counts (40/L) with lymphocytes predominating, red blood cells (16/L), high protein (2.09 g/L), and low glucose (40 mg/dL)... Blood cultures did not detect any growth.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Cryptococcal meningitis is a major consideration in subacute meningoencephalitis with elevated intracranial pressure, cranial neuropathies, and lymphocytic CSF pleocytosis with low glucose. However, cryptococcal infection occurs predominantly in severely immunocompromised hosts, particularly individuals with advanced HIV/AIDS or immunosuppressive therapy. This patient was an immunocompetent young adult with non-reactive HIV serology. Furthermore, the prominent exudative enhancement localized specifically to the basal meninges with secondary obstructive hydrocephalus is classic for tuberculous basal arachnoiditis rather than cryptococcal disease, which typically causes gelatinous pseudocysts or increased opening pressure without intense basilar inflammatory enhancement.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Both were negative for cytomegalovirus (CMV), toxoplasmosis IgM, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) serology... repeat contrast CT of the brain showed the development of ventriculomegaly suggestive of obstructive hydrocephalus and basilar enhancement

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Viral central nervous system infections frequently cause subacute headache, altered mental status, seizures, and CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis. However, viral meningoencephalitides typically exhibit normal CSF glucose levels (CSF-to-serum glucose ratio >0.60) and mild-to-moderate protein elevations (rarely exceeding 1.0–1.5 g/L). In this patient, marked CSF hypoglycorrhachia (glucose 40 mg/dL, CSF-to-serum ratio <50%), very high CSF protein (2.09 g/L), negative CMV serology, and pronounced basilar leptomeningeal enhancement causing obstructive hydrocephalus and severe hyponatremia strongly argue against viral meningoencephalitis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: high protein (2.09 g/L), and low glucose (40 mg/dL). The cerebral fluid to serum glucose ratio was less than 50%. Both were negative for cytomegalovirus (CMV), toxoplasmosis IgM, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) serology.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Neurosarcoidosis is a non-caseating granulomatous disease that can present with chronic basilar leptomeningeal enhancement, multiple cranial neuropathies (such as cranial nerve III or VII palsy), and hydrocephalus. However, neurosarcoidosis is a non-infectious inflammatory disorder that rarely causes sustained high fevers (38–39 °C) or rapid clinical deterioration with seizures within one week of presentation. Furthermore, severe CSF hypoglycorrhachia (40 mg/dL, <50% serum ratio) is atypical for sarcoidosis, and systemic screening revealed no evidence of hilar lymphadenopathy or parenchymal lung involvement on chest radiography.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: He reported a 12-day history of fevers (38-39 C), headaches, photosensitivity, diplopia, and severe fatigue... A chest x-ray indicated no pathology or localized consolidation

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Diagnostic Pivot: Tuberculous Meningitis (Tuberculosis / Mycobacterium tuberculosis)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot is established by synthesizing the triad of subacute indolent tempo (>5 days) in a young adult, cranial nerve involvement (third nerve palsy), characteristic CSF parameters (clear appearance, lymphocytic predominance, protein >1 g/L at 2.09 g/L, and marked hypoglycorrhachia <2.2 mmol/L / ratio <50%), refractory hyponatremia (SIADH / cerebral salt wasting), and diagnostic neuroimaging revealing thick basilar leptomeningeal enhancement with obstructive hydrocephalus (ventriculomegaly involving the lateral, third, and fourth ventricles). Applying standardized international consensus research case definitions, this constellation fulfills criteria for probable tuberculous meningitis with a definitive score of 12.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Based on well-established case definition criteria of tuberculous meningitis research, the patient was diagnosed with probable tuberculous meningitis with a total score of 12, which includes clinical criteria (symptom duration of more than five days (4), cranial nerve palsy (1)), cerebrospinal fluid criteria (clear appearance (1), lymphocytic predominance (1), protein concentration greater than one g/L (1), absolute cerebrospinal fluid glucose concentration less than 2.2 mmol/L (1)), cerebral imaging criteria (hydrocephalus (1), basal meningeal enhancement (2)).
